title: Imports, Exports and the Loader
summary: A program's **import table** lists every function it uses from DLLs; a DLL's **export table** lists every function it offers. Together they are a map of what a program can do and how its modules connect. This lesson reads both, explains the **import address table** that the loader fills in at start-up, and shows how to convert RVAs to file offsets so tables can be read from a file on disk.
markdown:
## Why imports matter so much For a reverse engineer, the import table is often the most informative part of a program. A program that imports `CreateFileW`, `ReadFile` and `CryptDecrypt` reads and decrypts files; one importing `WSAStartup` and `send` uses the network; one importing `CreateWindowExW` has a window. Before reading a single instruction, the imports outline what the program does. Tools list them first for this reason: ```powershell dumpbin /imports game.exe dumpbin /exports plugin.dll ``` ## The import table Data directory 1 (lesson 9.02) points at an array of **import descriptors**, one per DLL, ending with an all-zero entry: | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `Name` | RVA of the DLL's name, such as `"KERNEL32.dll"` | | `OriginalFirstThunk` | RVA of the **import lookup table**: what to import | | `FirstThunk` | RVA of the **import address table** (IAT): where the addresses go | Each lookup table entry is 8 bytes. If the top bit is set, the function is imported by **ordinal** (a number); otherwise the entry is the RVA of a **hint/name** entry: a 2-byte hint followed by the function's name, `"CreateFileW\0"`. ```mermaid flowchart LR D["Import descriptor
KERNEL32.dll"] --> ILT["Lookup table
→ 'CreateFileW'
→ 'ReadFile'
→ 0"] D --> IAT["Import address table
(on disk: same as lookup table)
(after loading: real addresses)"] IAT --> K["kernel32!CreateFileW
kernel32!ReadFile"] ``` ## What the loader does When the program starts (lesson 1.06), the loader, for each import descriptor: 1. loads the DLL (finding it by the search order, lesson 5.08) if it is not already loaded; 2. for each function in the lookup table, finds its address in the DLL's export table; 3. writes that address into the corresponding slot of the **IAT**. The program's code never contains the address of `CreateFileW` itself. Every call to an imported function goes **through** the IAT: ```asm call qword ptr [__imp_CreateFileW] ; read the address from the IAT slot, then call it ``` So in disassembly, calls to imported functions are indirect calls through a fixed set of memory slots, and disassemblers label them with the function names, which makes them easy landmarks. After loading, the IAT is made read-only, so it cannot be changed by accident. ## The export table A DLL's data directory 0 points at its **export directory**, which holds three parallel arrays: | Array | Holds | |---|---| | `AddressOfFunctions` | RVAs of the exported functions, indexed by ordinal minus the base | | `AddressOfNames` | RVAs of the exported names, sorted alphabetically so they can be binary-searched | | `AddressOfNameOrdinals` | For each name, the index into the functions array | `GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage")` (lesson 4.05) binary-searches the names, takes the matching ordinal index, and returns `module + AddressOfFunctions[index]`. An export can also be **forwarded**: its "address" points at a string such as `"NTDLL.RtlAllocateHeap"`, meaning "this function really lives in another DLL". Many `kernel32.dll` exports are forwarders. ## RVA to file offset All these tables use RVAs, which are offsets **in memory**. To read them from the file on disk, convert each RVA through the section table (lesson 9.02): find the section whose range contains the RVA, then > file offset = RVA − section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData because a section's bytes are at `VirtualAddress` in memory and at `PointerToRawData` in the file. An RVA that falls in no section's file data (for example in zero-filled `.bss` space) has no file offset. The practice task writes this function; every PE tool has it at its core. ## Reading your own imports at run time A loaded module's tables are already in memory at `module + RVA`, with no conversion needed: ```cpp #include #include #include int main() { auto* base{ reinterpret_cast(GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) }; const auto* nt{ reinterpret_cast(base + reinterpret_cast(base)->e_lfanew) }; const IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY dir{ nt->OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT] }; bool importsKernel32{ false }; int dlls{ 0 }; for (auto* d{ reinterpret_cast(base + dir.VirtualAddress) }; d->Name != 0; ++d) { ++dlls; std::string name{ reinterpret_cast(base + d->Name) }; if (_stricmp(name.c_str(), "KERNEL32.dll") == 0) importsKernel32 = true; } std::cout << "imports from several DLLs: " << (dlls >= 1 ? "yes" : "no") << ", including KERNEL32.dll: " << (importsKernel32 ? "yes" : "no") << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` imports from several DLLs: yes, including KERNEL32.dll: yes ``` ## Delay-load and dynamic imports Not every DLL a program uses appears in its import table. **Delay-loaded** DLLs (lesson 5.08) have their own table (data directory 13), and anything loaded with `LoadLibraryW` and `GetProcAddress` at run time appears only as strings in the program, which is why reverse engineers search for DLL and function names among a program's strings (lesson 9.06) as well as reading the import table. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Reading table RVAs as file offsets > Convert through the section table first, or the tables will appear to contain garbage. > [!warning] Assuming every import is by name > Entries with the top bit set are imported by ordinal; there is no name to read. > [!warning] Concluding a program never uses a function because it is not imported > It may be loaded at run time with `GetProcAddress`. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What does the loader write into the import address table? + The real addresses of the imported functions, found in each DLL's export table - The names of the functions - The program's own functions > Calls to imports go through these slots. ? How does a call to an imported function look in disassembly? + An indirect call through a memory slot, such as `call qword ptr [__imp_CreateFileW]` - A direct call to the DLL's address - A jump to the import descriptor > The code reads the address from the IAT at run time. ? A section has VirtualAddress 0x5000 and PointerToRawData 0x3400. What is the file offset of RVA 0x5120? + 0x3520 - 0x5120 - 0x8520 > 0x5120 − 0x5000 + 0x3400. ? What is a forwarded export? + An export entry that refers to a function in another DLL, by name - A function exported twice - A function that has been removed > Many kernel32 exports forward to ntdll. ```
ideas:
- Run `dumpbin /imports` on your own game and on a large application, and guess what each does from its imports alone.
- Extend the example to print each imported function name for KERNEL32.dll, following `OriginalFirstThunk` to the hint/name entries.
- Run `dumpbin /exports C:\Windows\System32\kernel32.dll` and find a forwarded export.

cards.q: What three things does an import descriptor point to?
cards.a: The DLL's name, the import lookup table (which functions, by name or ordinal) and the import address table (where the loader writes their addresses).

cards.q: How does `GetProcAddress` find a function by name?
cards.a: It binary-searches the export table's sorted name array, takes the corresponding ordinal index, and returns the module base plus that function's RVA.

cards.q: How do you convert an RVA to a file offset?
cards.a: Find the section containing the RVA, then compute RVA − the section's VirtualAddress + its PointerToRawData.
